title: M45 Pleiades
caption: The Pleiades (M45), imaged by the WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope
credit: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage), R. Cool (University of Arizona) and WIYN

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Blue haze surrounds the brightest stars of the Pleiades, M45, an open star cluster in Taurus that is easy to see without a telescope. The cluster is dominated by several hot, luminous, massive stars.

That blue glow is not gas lit up from within. It is starlight, mostly blue, bouncing off dust grains in the interstellar gas that lies between us and the stars. Blue light scatters more readily than red, which is also part of the reason Earth's daytime sky is blue.
An open cluster is a loose group of stars born together from the same cloud. The Pleiades also go by other names. They are often called the Seven Sisters, and in Japan the cluster is called Subaru.

understand.summary: The WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used three filters. B is shown in blue, V in green and I in red.
filters: 436 nm · Optical B (WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
537 nm · Optical V (WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
805 nm · Optical I (WIYN 0.9-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
understand.eye: The naked eye sees the cluster's bright stars, but the faint blue dust haze shows up only in long exposures. The I filter also records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.
